questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the philosophical foundation of the Declaration of Independence
questions.stem: In an amateur astronomer's log dated July 1776, which principle did the Declaration mainly assert about government?

options.text: Government exists to protect natural rights and derives power from consent
Government should be run by a single hereditary monarch for stability
options.misconception: confuses monarchy with the Declaration's rejection of it

options.text: Citizens owe unlimited obedience to any established legal authority
options.misconception: mistakes the Declaration for a defense of passive obedience

options.text: Rights are granted by the crown and can be revoked at will
options.misconception: reverses the source of rights from people to monarch

questions.explanation: The Declaration argues that governments are instituted to secure natural rights and derive just power from consent. The tempting wrong ideas defend monarchy or unlimited obedience, which the document rejects.
questions.hint: Think about consent of the governed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Articles created a weak central government
questions.stem: An astronomer's notebook asks why the Articles of Confederation left the central government unable to tax or regulate trade.

answer.exemplar: The Articles deliberately kept power with the states, so Congress could not levy taxes or control commerce, forcing it to request funds from states and leaving debts unpaid.

questions.explanation: Fear of centralized authority led states to withhold taxing power from Congress. Without revenue or trade control, the government could not pay debts or resolve interstate disputes.
questions.hint: Focus on state sovereignty under the Articles.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main purpose of the Constitutional Convention

stimulus.body: Delegates gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise the Articles of Confederation. Instead they drafted an entirely new frame of government with a stronger executive and bicameral legislature. Many delegates feared both anarchy and tyranny.

questions.stem: An observer's field notes record that delegates met in 1787; what outcome did the Convention actually produce?

options.text: A revised Articles of Confederation with only minor tax changes
options.misconception: underestimates the scope of the new Constitution

options.text: A new Constitution creating a stronger federal government
An immediate abolition of all state governments
options.misconception: exaggerates federal supremacy beyond the design

options.text: A treaty alliance with European powers for protection
options.misconception: confuses diplomatic aims with constitutional reform

questions.explanation: The Convention abandoned revision and produced a new Constitution with a stronger federal structure. The wrong options either minimize the change or invent unrelated outcomes.
